headline: Highest risk is medium: shared filesystem/MCP and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict pathways between Gemini CLI and oh-my-openagent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Gemini CLI can read/write repo files and use MCP; oh-my-openagent also touches project files and uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks. That creates a plausible shared-channel injection path where one agent’s output can be parsed by the other as instructions. The pair is not documented directly, so uncertainty pushes upward from low.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace or repo checkout, injected instructions can cross from one agent to the other.
IF either agent consumes file contents or MCP output as trusted instructions, prompt injection becomes reachable.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories.
Disable MCP servers not explicitly needed for the task.
Require provenance tags on any file or MCP payload before parsing it as instructions.
Use read-only mode for one agent during review tasks.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Gemini CLI reads user-provided directories and repo files, while oh-my-openagent touches project code, session history, and provider auth data. If they share a workspace or account context, sensitive files can flow into both agents’ outputs. The profiles show broad egress on both sides, so leakage is plausible in default use, though not proven directly.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same repository or home-directory workspace, file contents can be exposed to both.
IF either agent forwards its context to external APIs, sensitive project or auth data can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Run the agents in separate OS users or containers.
Exclude secrets files and auth configs from both workspaces.
Turn off network egress for one agent during sensitive tasks.
Use separate provider accounts and API keys.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace ACLs and secret redaction in the launcher.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Gemini CLI can execute shell, write the filesystem, and modify git state; oh-my-openagent can spawn subprocesses and has full-permissions mode. Both therefore can mutate the same repo or installation state, and the rubric treats unrestricted shared writes without locks as high risk. No locking or coordination primitive is documented, so uncertainty does not reduce severity.
conditions: IF both agents target the same git checkout, concurrent writes can corrupt state or overwrite work.
IF both agents run without an external lock, one agent can race the other on shared files.
mitigations: Run only one agent at a time on a shared repo.
Use separate clones for each agent.
Add a file lock around git and filesystem writes.
Keep one agent read-only during analysis.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control and conflict detection.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Gemini CLI can produce code and shell actions, and oh-my-openagent can use browser, LSP, and team actions. If oh-my-openagent treats Gemini’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into edits or messages. The pairwise handoff is inferred rather than directly documented, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent consumes Gemini CLI output without verification, incorrect facts can propagate into downstream actions.
IF Gemini CLI generates code or commands that oh-my-openagent executes, a single mistake can affect multiple work products.
mitigations: Require human review before execution or sending messages.
Insert a verification step between agents.
Limit Gemini output to structured, machine-checkable formats.
Disable downstream action tools for one agent during handoff.
requires-engineering: add provenance and confidence scoring to inter-agent messages.

E_compliance.rationale: Gemini CLI handles source code, files in cwd, and shell environment; oh-my-openagent handles session history, project code, and provider auth prompts. Both also use broad network egress, so the pair can move regulated or sensitive data across different retention and residency regimes. No specific certifications or DPA details are provided, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated data is present in the workspace, both agents may process it under different logging or retention policies.
IF either agent sends data to external providers, residency or DPA constraints may be violated.
mitigations: Do not place regulated data in shared workspaces.
Review each agent’s retention and logging settings.
Use region-locked provider endpoints where available.
Separate accounts for different compliance domains.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data-class routing and residency.
